comparison: Perfect agreement on manipulation check (C23, C26, C27). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers found the hunger manipulation valid and well-supported by RM-ANOVA results and control measures. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on PCA analysis (C28-C31, C103-C104). Both evaluations accepted the orthogonal taste/health framework with 81% variance explained. OpenEval provided detailed statistical justification while peer reviewers implicitly accepted it without question.

Strong agreement on main behavioral finding (C2, C18, C43, C76, C80). Both evaluations endorsed the core result that hunger increases taste-driven choices. OpenEval emphasized preregistered hypothesis confirmation with GLMM statistics; peer reviewers described it as an 'important study' with no concerns raised.

Perfect agreement on RT findings (C37-C40, C44-C45). Both evaluations accepted the GLMM results showing taste value difference and choice type effects without hunger state effects on RT. Peer reviewers implicitly endorsed through praise of modeling work incorporating RT data.

Strong agreement on attribute-specific attention effects (C49-C51, C89). Both evaluations supported the eye-tracking findings. OpenEval emphasized robustness to outlier exclusion; peer reviewers noted attentional mechanisms as a strength without critique.

Strong agreement on attentional mediation (C3, C19, C60, C77-C78, C88). Both evaluations affirmed the mediation mechanism. OpenEval provided detailed Bayesian mediation statistics; peer reviewers described 'compelling evidence' and noted formal mediation by relative dwell time.

Perfect agreement on model comparison (C5, C20, C61, C65-C66). Both evaluations praised the systematic model comparison showing maaDDM2φ superiority. OpenEval detailed DIC, convergence, and posterior predictive checks; peer reviewers called the modeling 'impressive in its rigor' and 'state-of-the-art.'

Strong agreement on attribute weighting mechanism (C6, C21, C63, C68, C122). Both evaluations accepted the dual mechanism interpretation. OpenEval emphasized parameter estimates with credible intervals; peer reviewers accepted the mechanistic interpretation without challenge.

Strong agreement on attribute-specific attentional discounting (C7, C21, C64, C96-C99, C122). Both evaluations supported the model extension isolating hunger effects to health information. OpenEval detailed parameter estimates for φH vs φT; peer reviewers endorsed the noisy accumulation model with attribute discounting.

Agreement on predictive relationships (C32-C33, C82-C83). Both evaluations accepted that taste and health ratings predict choices. OpenEval integrated these into broader behavioral findings; peer reviewers noted this as a strength without concerns.

Agreement on limitation but both uncertain (C106-C109). Both evaluations acknowledged demand effects as a concern. OpenEval noted inability to exclude effects on parameters; Reviewer 2 wanted first-session-only analysis but was partially reassured by order effects analysis. Neither could definitively rule out demand effects.

Divergence on normative interpretation (C113-C115). OpenEval rated uncertain due to lack of direct measurement of homeostatic vs hedonic mechanisms. Reviewer 4 questioned whether observed behavior represents suboptimal choice or healthy adaptive response, expressing ambiguity about the adaptive/maladaptive characterization.

Partial overlap on intervention implications (C116-C117). OpenEval rated uncertain due to speculative leap to intervention efficacy without direct testing. Reviewer 4's concern about adaptive vs maladaptive interpretation relates to whether interventions are even warranted, questioning the premise rather than the mechanism.

Perfect agreement on methodological contribution (C123-C124). Both evaluations praised the model extension. OpenEval noted superior fit and applicability to other contexts; Reviewer 2 explicitly commended the rigor and innovation of testing 8 DDM variants including new maaDDM2φ.

Strong agreement on methodological rigor (C125-C128, C16). Both evaluations endorsed preregistration, power analysis, and sample size justification. OpenEval detailed conservative effect size estimation; Reviewer 3 explicitly noted well-powered sample and preregistration as strengths.

OpenEval found robustness analyses using wanting and caloric measures (C101-C102) supported the main findings through convergent evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addressed these supplementary analyses.

OpenEval found literature contextualization (C85-C86) appropriate, noting apt comparison to Fisher & Rangel (2014) and novel extension to state-dependent effects. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addressed this contextualization.

OpenEval rated explanations for dwell time asymmetry (C90-C95) as uncertain, noting plausible but largely inferential information complexity account without ruling out alternatives. No corresponding peer review evaluation addressed this specific interpretation.

OpenEval found comprehensive experimental design documentation (C16-C17, C130-C140) well-supported and methodologically sound. Peer reviewers praised design elements but did not provide a separate evaluation of the documentation completeness itself.

OpenEval found analytical approaches (C141-C143, C145-C146) well-documented and appropriate, including preprocessing, GLMM specifications, Bayesian methods, and convergence diagnostics. No corresponding peer review evaluation separately assessed these analytical documentation claims.

OpenEval found the synthesis of main findings (C79, C87, C105, C121) appropriately characterized the 'twofold mechanism' with convergent evidence. Peer reviewers endorsed individual findings but did not provide a separate evaluation of the synthesis itself.

OpenEval rated speculation about working memory and attentional discounting (C100) as uncertain, noting it was explicitly speculative and lacked direct empirical support. No corresponding peer review evaluation addressed this specific speculation.
